candidates.title: Ask HN: What is the proper way of preventing AI labs to use your private data
candidates.raw_content: Recent discussions show that most people (including myself) are uneducated about the privacy policies of these AI companies. People talk about the "opt-out" button in the settings and assume this will be enough. But even the text on the toggle implies this is not the full story. ChatGPT: "Improve the model for everyone" (But are they free to use my data internally, i.e. "not for everyone") Claude: "Help improve our AI models" (When you click Learn More [0], they admit they may use them to train internal security models etc. if their security classifiers they run on every conversation flag us [with what criteria]) On top of that Codex and Claude Code have different security options and basically they can gain access to everything we have. What is an easy way to do a proper setup for consumer subscriptions. candidates.raw_content: Hey people! I have been compiling a directory of AI API providers which provide a combined total of $4.3k in free API credits and I'm super proud of it so far. It serves as a community-curated directory. Everyone can review, upvote and edit API providers to keep the directory honest and accurate. After tons of hours I've managed to compile a database of 310 API providers. The directory also allows you to link all 310 API providers, to create one OpenAI- and Claude-compatible gateway then route any model, through any vendor - via a single URL with failover aliases, daily spend caps and per-request compute metering you can audit line by line. I have not found another project that offers an organized, community-curated system for AI API providers on the same scale as this one. There is a submission feature so you can submit your favorite AI API providers for free. Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49641128 Points: 3 # Comments: 0

candidates.title: this is a very good and well designed report however, two impt assumptions in it that significantly change the analysis once you start to play with it: 1. the report assumes that jobs can be decomposed into tasks 2. the report models human tasks created by automation always as a fraction of automated tasks. in other words, the underlying assumptions is automation always reduces human labor (or at best leaves it the same) taken in reverse order: does automation always reduce human work? in my experience, the answer is no. automation often creates multiples more work for humans. i have a full argument here (https://t.co/Lb7SUCe2pO) for why this is structurally true. but i think any honest analysis of the economic impacts of AI has to take work creation seriously. can jobs be decomposed into tasks? yes, that is a useful lens. but lists of tasks is a way of looking at jobs—one that makes the question of how much of a job is automatable actually tractable. therefore, it's useful. but this is not the full picture, it's just jobs as exposed to our method of questioning. a good example: under this model, where do the new tasks come from? are they just from bosses that add a list to the task list for workers to complete? where do those tasks come from? unless you can model that well you are missing a key term in the analysis (see the first point above.) another way of looking at this, borrowing from wittgenstein and heidegger, is that a job is a particular way of seeing and caring about the world. an editor notices things a nurse doesn’t, and vice versa. what you care about shapes what you notice, what seems worth doing, and what counts as doing it well. you can make some of that explicit as a task list. but as your tools and circumstances change, the same cares can generate entirely new tasks. that process is part of the job. the above is completely missing from this analysis (understandably because it's, by definition, very hard to model!) but if you take it seriously, it shoudl substantially change your perspective automation and jobs

candidates.title: The way to the reconcile capability level of AI vs. GDP impact is that the diffusion of AI will take much longer than people think. And it will also show up in ways that are hard to measure in GDP immediately. You could bring the world’s greatest superintelligence to many workflows, and still be bound by the laws of corporate physics: getting data prepared and put into a pipeline, process reengineering and change management, aligning on how the new workflow should function, and so on. Even after you solve all that, you’re still bound by the speed of the real world: waiting for a customer to respond to a proposal, getting a permit for a project, a drug discovery pipeline taking years to eventually reach the consumer, and so on. Not to mention lots of positive daily AI use-cases are entirely net neutral to GDP, at least in the near term. AI diffusion is going to be the theme of the next decade. The upside is that there’s a tremendous amount of opportunity in building the bridges between superintelligence and real-world workflows.
